title: Magnetic Properties of Materials — 20 MCQs
description: Topics: permeability, susceptibility, dia/para/ferro magnetism, hysteresis, Curie temperature, B–H behaviour, soft/hard magnetic materials.

questions.q: Relative permeability μ_r of a material is defined as:
options: μ/μ0 (ratio of material permeability to vacuum)
questions.explanation: μ_r = μ/μ0; μ is permeability of material, μ0 vacuum permeability.

questions.q: Magnetic susceptibility χ_m relates to permeability by which relation (SI)?
questions.explanation: In linear media B = μ0(1+χ_m)H so μ_r = 1 + χ_m.

questions.q: For a diamagnetic material, the magnetic susceptibility χ_m is typically:
questions.explanation: Diamagnets create induced magnetization opposite to applied field → small negative susceptibility.

questions.q: Paramagnetic materials show which behaviour in a magnetic field?
options: Small positive susceptibility; magnetization in direction of applied field
questions.explanation: Paramagnets have unpaired moments aligning partially with applied B giving small positive χ.

questions.q: Ferromagnetic materials differ from paramagnets because they:
options: Exhibit spontaneous magnetization and can have very large positive susceptibilities
questions.explanation: Ferromagnets show spontaneous ordering below Curie temperature and high permeability.

questions.q: Curie temperature (T_C) is:
options: The temperature above which a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic
questions.explanation: Above T_C thermal agitation destroys long-range order; material becomes paramagnetic.

questions.q: Initial (or intrinsic) relative permeability refers to:
options: μ_r at very small applied H near zero
questions.explanation: Initial permeability is slope of B–H curve near origin before significant magnetization.

questions.q: Saturation magnetization means:
options: All magnetic domains aligned and further H produces little additional B
questions.explanation: Saturation occurs when most domains aligned; B approaches saturation value.

questions.q: Magnetic hysteresis refers to:
options: Non-reversible B–H loop showing history dependence (remanence & coercivity)
questions.explanation: Hysteresis loop shows B vs H path differs for magnetizing and demagnetizing; defines remanent flux and coercive field.

questions.q: Coercivity (H_c) of a ferromagnet is:
options: The negative applied field needed to reduce magnetization to zero after saturation
questions.explanation: Coercive field quantifies how strongly a material retains magnetization; high H_c = hard magnetic material.

questions.q: Remanence (residual magnetization) is:
options: Magnetization remaining when applied H is reduced to zero
questions.explanation: Remanent magnetization is B or M left after removing applied field.

questions.q: Soft magnetic materials (e.g., transformer core) are characterized by:
options: Low coercivity, low hysteresis loss, high permeability
High coercivity and high hysteresis loss
questions.explanation: Soft materials easily magnetize/demagnetize with small hysteresis — good for AC cores.

questions.q: Hard magnetic materials (permanent magnets) are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Hard magnets retain magnetization (large H_c and remanence) suitable for permanent magnets.

questions.q: Relative susceptibility χ_m,r (often just χ) is related to magnetization M and H by:
questions.explanation: Magnetization M (A/m) = χ_m H for linear media; B = μ0 (H + M) = μ0 (1+χ_m) H.

questions.q: For linear isotropic magnetic materials B and H are related by:
questions.explanation: B = μ H and μ = μ0 μ_r; for linear media μ constant.

questions.q: In ferromagnets domain theory explains hysteresis because:
options: Domains reorient irreversibly over energy barriers; reversing H needs work (coercivity)
questions.explanation: Domain wall motion and pinning by defects cause hysteresis and energy dissipation.

questions.q: Temperature dependence of susceptibility for paramagnets approximately follows:
questions.explanation: Curie law gives χ = C/T for simple paramagnets (C Curie constant) at not-too-low temperatures.

questions.q: Diamagnetic materials (e.g., bismuth, copper) have which characteristic?
options: Induced magnetization opposite applied field, weak and temperature independent
questions.explanation: Diamagnetism arises from Lenz-type induced currents; effect weak and typically negative χ nearly independent of T.

questions.q: If a material has relative permeability μ_r ≈ 1 and small positive χ, it is likely:
questions.explanation: Paramagnets have μ_r slightly greater than 1 (small positive susceptibility).

questions.q: Which experimental feature distinguishes ferromagnetism from paramagnetism?
options: Presence of hysteresis loop and spontaneous magnetization below T_C
questions.explanation: Ferromagnets show spontaneous order and hysteresis; paramagnets are linear and reversible.
